The three boards form a chain: power board → main board → sensor board. Because the main board is in the middle, it receives power from the power board through J\_PWR\_PWR, uses that power locally, AND forwards it to the sensor board through J\_SENSOR\_PWR. \- Keep the series resistor footprint DNP because the LED strip limits itself
\- Do not add a flyback diode, since the LED is resistive rather than inductive

At worst, the current will be ~70mA, based on a 5W/m strip × 67mm cut, which is comfortably below the BSS138's 200mA rating.

The 3V3 jumper and DNP series R footprint are included solely as a fallback for a possible future bare-LED configuration; leaving both empty now adds no cost.

The complete specification is in [URL_016], within the J\_DISP\_LED rows / pinout / Critical Routing.

To recap, the factory tested all 3 boards: 1 works and has L3 stable at 3.3V, while the other 2 fluctuate between 0.5–2V. That suggests the design is fine and that those 2 may have an AXP2101 thermal-pad soldering problem.

The factory uses a completely automated process with a stencil + reflow oven and no hand soldering. I reviewed the gerbers, and the 13 tented GND vias beneath the pad appear fine. However, the paste aperture for the AXP2101 thermal pad is one full, unsegmented opening. Could excessive paste cause the chip to float in the reflow oven and make inconsistent ground contact? Would dividing that pad into a segmented "windowpane" paste aperture improve the yield?
What is your opinion?

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: I noticed one additional detail that may support this theory. According to the factory, VBUS and VSYS are normal on all 3 boards, and all of those pins are located along the top edge of the AXP2101. The DCDC1 pins—FB1, LX1, and VIN1—are all on the right edge, which is precisely the side that fails on the 2 defective boards. This makes it seem as though the chip tilts during reflow: the top edge remains connected while the right edge lifts. That is why I suspect the single full paste opening beneath the center pad may be depositing too much solder and causing the chip to float. Is that consistent with what you would expect, and can you update the stencil to a windowpane pattern on your side?
